2.1 **The transition matrix and duality at $1$.** Write $D_{A,B}=d_{A,B}(1)=[M(B):L(A)]$ with simple rows and standard columns. Then $[M(B)]=\sum_A D_{A,B}[L(A)]$, so it is the simple-to-standard expansion that uses $D^{-1}$. BGG reciprocity instead gives $[P(A):M(B)]=D_{A,B}$, hence $[P(A)]=\sum_BD_{A,B}[M(B)]$; this matrix is the transposed standard/simple multiplicity array when rows are projective labels, not its inverse. Under the standard-class map these are exactly the defining $P_A$ and $L_A$ expansions. On the actual finite type-$A$ cuts, each nonconstant term of the quasi-$R$ root-factor expansion has a factor $s-s^{-1}$ and coefficients regular at $s=1$ (the quantum-factorial denominators have nonzero ordinary-factorial values there). Thus the tensor bar matrix specializes to the identity; passage to the primitive wedge factors preserves this specialization. The source monomial Gram matrices, which are its inverse, are consequently the identity at $1$. Multiplying the $D$ projective array by the $D^{-1}$ simple array yields $\langle P_A,L_B\rangle=\delta_{AB}$. No inverse BGG multiplicity matrix is asserted. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

literal_current_use_locations.text: 1.3 **The parameter-one normalization and label bijections.** At parameter one the quasi-canonical family satisfies $P_A=T_{A^\uparrow}$ and the costandard family is $D_A=\pi_{\mathrm{Fock}}L_A$ with $A\mapsto A^\uparrow$ the rectification from reverse-standard to standard tableaux and $\downarrow$ its inverse, by [[thm-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule-has-the-qg-global-bases]] and [[def-dual-canonical-canonical-and-quasi-canonical-fock-bases]]; this gives (iv). [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 **The decomposition formula (i).** The formula $[S(B)]=\sum_{A\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda}d_{A,B}(1)[D(A)]$ for every $B\in\mathrm{Col}^\Lambda$ is the standard-class half of the identification of step 1.1; the coefficient dictionary $M_B=\sum_Ad_{A,B}(s)L_A$, $P_A=\sum_Bd_{A,B}(s)M_B$ is that of [[def-dual-canonical-canonical-and-quasi-canonical-fock-bases]], and the full polynomial transition matrix, its unitriangularity and the restriction to standard simple labels are those of [[thm-parabolic-kl-polynomials-give-the-dual-canonical-transition-matrix]] and [[thm-standard-tableau-monomials-form-a-basis-of-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule]]. This proves (i); no off-standard label is made a simple class. [step 1.1, F1, given, algebra]

2.3 **Arbitrary consecutive $I$.** Let $I$ be any nonempty consecutive set (possibly unbounded above or below), fix a content $\alpha$ and a finite list of residue operations, and choose a finite lower endpoint $k$ and upper endpoint $r$ so that the LETTER alphabet $[k,r+1]$ contains every charge and the ROOT interval $[k,r]$ contains the support of $\alpha$ and every shifted support occurring in the operations. The common-tail and double-cut compatibility of [[thm-standard-tableau-monomials-form-a-basis-of-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule]] and [[thm-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule-has-the-qg-global-bases]], together with the contractible-central-corner restriction of [[def-the-higher-level-schur-weyl-projective-generator-and-schur-functor]] and [[thm-higher-level-schur-weyl-double-centralizer]], shows that added bottom occupancy is maximal in every column (so every new entry is forced ground) and added top occupancy is zero, and that the monomial, bar, global and projected basis equations are unchanged on the selected finite weight set. Hence the Hecke block is the same content component of the same $H_d(m)$, with the same intrinsic Specht modules, projective and simple labels, residue projectors and residue maps, and the blockwise statements of (i)-(iv) glue along these compatible finite pieces to give the arbitrary-$I$ statement. At the level of the block decomposition of the tower, the excluded blocks for $I\ne\mathbb Z$ are real (the supported cut is proper by [[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-tower-and-residue-functors]]), and no equality of $H^\Lambda$ with $\bigoplus_dH_d(m)$ is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, given, algebra]

literal_current_use_locations.text: 1.3 **The standard lattice and its ground generation.** The standard lattice $V(\Lambda)_{\mathbb Z}$ has $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{P_A:A\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda\}$, the source vector $P_A$ lies in the highest constituent with $\pi_{\mathrm{Fock}}P_A=P_A$, and at parameter one $P_A=T_{A^\uparrow}=s^{-a(\alpha)}G_{\mathrm{low}}(A)$, so $V(\Lambda)_{\mathbb Z}$ is integrally generated by its ground vector $P_{A_\Lambda}$ under the divided-power operators; this is the parameter-one specialization of [[thm-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule-has-the-qg-global-bases]], together with the basis statements of [[def-dual-canonical-canonical-and-quasi-canonical-fock-bases]] and [[thm-simples-projectives-and-tiltings-map-to-the-three-distinguished-fock-bases]]. [given, algebra]

literal_current_use_locations.text: 2.2 **The Specht classes.** For the intrinsic Specht module $S(B)=\pi(N(B))$ of step 1.1, apply the exact functor $\pi$ to a generalized-standard composition series of $N(B)$; exactness and [F2] give $[S(B)]=\sum_{A}[N(B):K(A)]\,[D(A)]$ in $G_0$, the sum running over the simples, i.e. over $A\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda$ by step 1.1. The multiplicity $[N(B):K(A)]$ equals the Fock coefficient $d_{A,B}(1)$ of step 1.2 by the O-side multiplicity dictionary of step 1.3 and the Schur-image theorem of step 1.1. Hence $\Phi([S(B)])=\sum_{A\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda}d_{A,B}(1)D_A=S_B$, and the square submatrix on standard columns is unitriangular, so $\{S_B:B\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda\}$ is an integral basis; this completes (i). [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F2, algebra]

2.3 **Divided-power integral forms.** The lower library global vectors $G_{\mathrm{low}}(A)=T_{A^\uparrow}=s^{-a(\alpha)}P_A$ and the form-dual upper vectors $G_{\mathrm{up}}(A)=s^{a(\alpha)}D_A$ with $a(\alpha)=(2\Lambda-\alpha,\alpha)/2$ span integral forms on which the divided powers of the Chevalley generators act integrally, by [[thm-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule-has-the-qg-global-bases]]; at parameter one the standard lattice is therefore generated over $\mathbb Z$ by its ground vector $P_{A_\Lambda}$ under the divided-power operators $f_i^{(n)}$, while the costandard lattice is generated by the ground vector $D_{A_\Lambda}$ over $\mathbb Q$ and is identified with the form-dual family by the same theorem. This gives the divided-power clause of (ii) and separates the two lattices. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.2 **Level zero.** If the level is $0$, then $\Lambda=0$, the only simple is the ground class in degree $0$, and the tower is $H^\Lambda_0=\mathbb C$ by the level-$0$ convention of [[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-tower-and-residue-functors]]; then $G_0=\mathbb Z[D(\varnothing)]\cong\mathbb ZD_\varnothing$ is the ground line alone, with no further costandard vectors, standard lattice or residue operators. This is the level-$0$ clause of (v). [step 1.1, step 2.1, given]
